response:
The central question is whether the geometry of polysemanticity in a trained network — specifically, how many features get packed into each neuron and how orthogonally they're arranged — changes systematically as you trade width for depth while holding parameter count roughly constant. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on residual stream or MLP activations give you an empirical handle on this: the density of active latents per token and the degree of feature overlap in the learned dictionary are measurable proxies for superposition load. The core tension is that wider networks have higher-dimensional activation spaces, which the geometry of Johnson-Lindenstrauss suggests should accommodate more nearly-orthogonal feature directions — but deeper networks may factorize features hierarchically across layers, potentially reducing the superposition pressure at any single layer even in lower-dimensional spaces.

What a beginner misses is that SAE reconstruction fidelity is not a neutral measuring instrument here — a poorly-fit SAE on a narrow-but-deep model might appear to show high superposition simply because the features it needs to recover are more compositional and harder for a shallow dictionary to decompose, not because the underlying model is genuinely packing more unrelated concepts into single directions. The expert worry is therefore about confounding the measurement artifact with the phenomenon: differences in SAE loss across width/depth regimes may reflect dictionary inadequacy rather than true shifts in superposition density, and controlling for this requires careful ablations on SAE width, sparsity penalty, and whether geometric measures (e.g., cosine similarity distributions among active decoder directions) track consistently with activation-space metrics.

In this regime, the decoder matrix columns will be forced into tighter angular packing simply due to the pigeonhole geometry: you're trying to place 16k unit vectors in a 512-dimensional space, where the maximum number of nearly-orthogonal directions is hard-capped around the dimension count. The measurable artifact is an inflation of pairwise cosine similarities among active decoder directions — you'll see the cosine similarity distribution shift rightward not because the model is doing more superposition, but because the dictionary literally has nowhere else to put the vectors. This masquerades as genuine superposition density increase because the standard diagnostic — high co-activation rates among nominally distinct SAE latents, or elevated mean cosine similarity among active features per token — is exactly what over-packing in a low-dimensional space produces, even if the underlying model has cleaner feature separation than a wider peer. Scherlis et al. The L1 penalty acts on the pre-activation magnitudes of SAE latents, and its effective bite depends on the typical scale of activations in the residual stream — which is not constant across architectures. In a narrower model, the residual stream has lower intrinsic dimensionality, meaning individual feature directions must carry more "load" per direction to represent the same information, which tends to inflate activation norms along those directions; the same L1 coefficient that produced, say, L0≈25 active latents per token on a wide model may now produce L0≈8 on the narrow-deep peer, not because the model is more sparse in any meaningful sense but because the penalty is now disproportionately expensive relative to the signal. The deeper model compounds this differently: if features are hierarchically composed across layers, any single layer's activations may genuinely be sparser because partial computations are distributed vertically — so low L0 at a middle layer could reflect architectural factorization rather than superposition relief. The dangerous interpretation is reading L0≈8 as "this model uses cleaner, more disentangled representations" when the correct reading might be "the SAE is under-reconstructing because the penalty is strangling latents that would have fired weakly but informationally." Conerly et al. in Anthropic's 2023 SAE scaling work implicitly flagged this when noting that reconstruction loss and sparsity trade off differently across model scales, suggesting the Pareto frontier itself shifts — meaning a fixed penalty coefficient doesn't hold you at a comparable operating point across architectures, it moves you to a qualitatively different regime on a differently-shaped curve.

Single-layer latent density is fundamentally a local measurement on a non-stationary signal — the residual stream at layer k of a deep model is not semantically comparable to layer k of a shallow model because the computation allocated to each layer differs, making cross-architecture comparisons at matched layer indices essentially meaningless without a theory of what each layer is "doing." If a concept like "indirect object in a prepositional phrase" is fully encoded in one MLP layer of a wide-shallow model but smeared across three successive attention and MLP layers in a narrow-deep model, the single-layer SAE on the wide model will show one dense multi-component latent cluster while the narrow model shows three sparse ones — and naively you'd conclude the narrow model has better disentanglement, which inverts the truth. The natural candidate for a depth-invariant aggregate is something like total latent energy per concept per token summed across all layers: for each ground-truth concept (identified by behavioral probes or circuits analysis), count the total number of SAE latents that activate for it across all layers, weighted by activation magnitude. Elhage et al.'s residual stream perspective in the "Mathematical Framework" paper (2021) gives the formal scaffolding for this — the residual stream is a summation channel, so a concept's full representational cost is the integral over depth, not any slice. The practical obstacle is that "concept identity" must be held constant across the sum, which requires either a shared probe that generalizes across layers (hard, because representations rotate) or a cross-layer dictionary that explicitly models how early-layer latents compose into late-layer ones — something like the cross-layer SAE variant explored informally in some Eleuther and Apollo Research work but not yet standardized. Without this aggregate, any width-vs-depth superposition comparison is comparing a photograph of a river at one point to a photograph at another and concluding one river carries more water.

A cross-layer dictionary needs its atoms to be defined in a layer-agnostic semantic space rather than in the coordinate frame of any particular residual stream, which means the encoder must learn a mapping from each layer's activation geometry into a shared concept manifold where the same feature has the same code regardless of whether it's expressed at layer 4 or layer 14. Formally, this requires something like an equivariance constraint: if a rotation R maps layer-k representations to layer-(k+1) representations for a given concept, the dictionary encoder should satisfy f(Rx) = f(x) for those concept-preserving rotations — but this is extremely hard to enforce without knowing R in advance, since the rotation is itself a learned, data-dependent quantity that varies by concept and context. The closest existing objective is the one used in universal or cross-model SAE work, where a shared dictionary is trained jointly on activations from multiple layers or models by concatenating or aligning activation spaces before decomposition — but alignment is typically done via linear regression or CKA-based matching, which only handles global rotation and doesn't account for the fact that the "same concept" may live in genuinely different subspaces at different depths due to superposition reshuffling. Anthropic's April 2025 "scaling and evaluating SAEs" work implicitly acknowledges this by showing that SAE feature absorption — where one latent subsumes another's role across training — gets worse at deeper layers, suggesting the dictionary atoms are not stable semantic units but layer-local compression artifacts. What no current objective enforces is semantic persistence: the requirement that if latent i in layer k and latent j in layer k+4 both causally mediate the same behavioral output (measurable by activation patching), they should be assigned the same dictionary atom — this would require a causal invariance loss term that ties dictionary identity to circuit-level function rather than geometric proximity, and no published SAE training objective includes this.

The most serious failure mode is causal conflation collapse: activation patching identifies latents that mediate the same output, but two latents can produce identical downstream effects via entirely different intermediate computations — one might suppress a competing feature while the other amplifies the target, and forcing them to share a dictionary atom would merge these mechanistically distinct operations into a single "concept unit" that is behaviorally coherent but computationally fictitious. This is not hypothetical; Wang et al.'s IOI circuit work (2022) already shows that name mover heads and backup name mover heads produce the same behavioral output through redundant but structurally distinct pathways, and a causal invariance loss would collapse these into one atom, destroying exactly the mechanistic resolution you want from interpretability. A second failure mode is temporal credit misassignment under composition: if layer-k latent A partially computes a concept that layer-(k+3) latent B completes, patching B causally implicates A (because A's output feeds B's input), so the causal invariance loss would force them to share an atom even though they represent genuinely different stages of a computation rather than the same concept at different depths — the dictionary would hallucinate a unified feature where there is actually a pipeline. The resulting dictionary would show artificially low atom count (appearing to have fewer, cleaner concepts than a single-layer SAE) while having dramatically worse reconstruction locality: each shared atom would need a complex, layer-dependent decoder direction to reconstruct the actual activations, violating the implicit assumption that dictionary atoms correspond to fixed geometric directions. Conerly et al.'s finding that feature splitting occurs as SAE width increases is the single-layer analogue — atoms that seemed unified at low dictionary size turn out to be conflations — and causal invariance loss would systematically re-introduce exactly this conflation at the cross-layer level by using behavioral equivalence as a proxy for representational identity, which it isn't.

The cleanest intervention is simultaneous multi-site patching with independence testing: rather than patching one latent and measuring output change, you patch pairs of candidate latents jointly and measure whether their causal contributions are subadditive (indicating redundancy — they implement the same output path) or additive/superadditive (indicating composition — they represent sequential stages of a single concept). If patching A alone moves logit difference by +0.8 and patching B alone moves it by +0.7, but patching both moves it by +0.9, the subadditivity signature identifies them as redundant backup implementations rather than compositional stages, which would show near-additivity or synergy. This is essentially the causal scrubbing logic from Chan et al. (2022) extended to cross-layer latent pairs — causal scrubbing already tests whether two nodes share a causal role by checking if resampling one while conditioning on the other leaves the output distribution unchanged, and this directly operationalizes the redundancy vs. composition distinction without requiring you to hand-specify the circuit topology. The scaling problem is severe: for a model with L layers and D SAE latents per layer, the number of pairs to test is O(L²D²), which for L=32 and D=16k reaches roughly 260 billion pairs — computationally impossible exhaustively on anything resembling GPT-4 scale. The practical path is hierarchical screening: first use cheap linear attribution methods (gradient×activation or integrated gradients) to prune the candidate pair set to latents with overlapping attribution mass on the same output token, then apply the subadditivity test only to the surviving ~0.1% of pairs — Nanda et al.'s ACDC work (2022) demonstrated that this kind of attribution-guided pruning can reduce circuit search space by 99%+ while recovering most causally relevant structure, suggesting the screening step is tractable even if the exhaustive version isn't.

Gradient attribution systematically underdiscovers saturated or near-binary latents — features that are either fully on or fully off at the operating point, where the local gradient is near zero even though the feature is causally critical, a direct consequence of the flat regions in ReLU and TopK activation functions used in modern SAEs. This means the screening step will preferentially select latent pairs that operate in their linear regime at the evaluation inputs, biasing the surviving candidate set toward features that are partially active and smoothly varying — which in practice means lower-frequency, more distributed features rather than sharp, sparse, high-confidence ones. The distortion this introduces into a width-vs-depth comparison is asymmetric: wider models tend to have more nearly-linear superposition (many weakly active features per token, as documented in Templeton et al.'s Claude 3 Sonnet SAE analysis showing L0≈200 at high-fidelity operating points) while narrower-deeper models may rely more heavily on sharp, near-saturated feature activations because lower-dimensional spaces reward high-confidence sparse codes — so gradient screening will recover a higher fraction of the causally relevant pairs in the wide model than in the narrow one. The causal invariance loss trained on this biased sample will therefore over-represent compositional cross-layer relationships in wide models and under-represent them in narrow ones, making narrow-deep models appear to have fewer cross-layer concept continuations — not because they genuinely have simpler hierarchical structure but because their causally important latents were invisible to the screener. The fix is well-known in attribution literature — integrated gradients (Sundararajan et al., 2017) or gradient×input with a meaningful baseline recover saturation-regime contributions by path-integrating through the activation curve — but applying integrated gradients to SAE latent pairs at scale reintroduces the computational cost that screening was meant to avoid, creating a fundamental tension between screening efficiency and attribution completeness.
